title: India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
content: Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August. But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention. Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions. "Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said. A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage. "The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said. Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment. But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes? India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control. But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat. Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods. Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important. A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period. Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online. Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau. The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily. And the dangers extend beyond flooding. A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms. While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau. The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress. The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations. Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas. In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet. Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project. But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort. "One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute. "What happened after that no one knows," he added. Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet. But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022. China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said. Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes. "These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group. But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved. One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value. "What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank. Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders. The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow. "There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD. He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks. Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay. "Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says. Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain. For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat. Rescue officials fear more people are buried under the debris in the north-western city of Peshawar. Cheshire East Council votes to object to the carbon capture proposals and write to the government. The Bollywood actor had been detained and released while participating in a protest in Mumbai on 10 October. The body was recovered from a large blue plastic storage container - locally called a drum. China is the North's largest trading partner and a lifeline against the sanctions Pyongyang faces. title: Eight crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
content: Eight of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a tanker ablaze off Romania's coast, naval authorities say. The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire on Thursday morning. Romanian President Nicușor Dan later confirmed it was struck by drones. The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks. A swarm of Russian drones was detected overnight not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island. Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port were hit during the sea crossing. It did not name the vessels. On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing. Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy. A search and rescue operation for the eight missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed. The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel. The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area. The tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT). Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader was hit by two drones. The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked. This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened. The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state." Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region. The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area. Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports. On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable". Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine. Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi. Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports. Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked. Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea. Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory . Buildings were set alight on the second day of demonstrations from thousands of students who want better university conditions and job prospects. The 71-year-old Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the 90-minute procedure on Tuesday. Four years after the attacks, Serhii Kuznetsov appears in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany. Elon Musk's system allows Kyiv to protect Ukrainian skies and effectively guide drones to Russian targets. With few details so far, it is unclear what might need to change for a Pope who has been focused on stability. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Wes Streeting in US for Hegseth meeting as Ukraine tensions escalate – UK politics live
content: Defence secretary Wes Streeting is in Washington DC to meet US counterpart Pete Hegseth at a sensitive time when relations between the two normally close allies are strained by tensions over Ukraine, Iran and the Middle East. The meeting is due to take place at lunchtime in the Pentagon a day after Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy visited London and said he felt betrayed by the US decision to throttle military access to the Starlink satellite internet system. The UK finds itself in the middle of the deepening US-Ukraine dispute, and on Wednesday prime minister Andy Burnham met Zelenskyy and promised that he would engage in “laying the ground” for a reconciliation with US president Donald Trump. At the same time, the UK faces questions about its ability to safeguard US military bases in Britain to the satisfaction of Hegseth, more than one of which has been targeted by Iran, leading to the recent withdrawal of 12 B-1 bombers from Fairford. The US is also weighing up whether it wants to help Saudi Arabia in the fast developing conflict with Yemen’s Houthis at a time when it is trying to step away from a fresh outbreak of fighting with Iran before midterm elections next month. That presents the UK with a difficult choice, because while the UK has largely kept out of the Iran war, it has acted as a junior partner with the US in joint in a series of air strikes on the Houthis during 2025 and early 2025. Labour recognises that engaging in fresh bombing in the Middle East could be a difficult sell to the British public when Trump’s war in Iran is being blamed for cost of living pressures and increased energy prices at home. Prior to meeting Hegseth, Streeting will also appear at the CSIS thinktank, at a session entitled “the future of UK-US defence cooperation”. Prior to his flight to the US, Streeting sidestepped the tricky geopolitical issues and emphasised that he hoped that in future “Britain and America can lead the next generation of defence innovation”. Amnesty International UK’s refugee and migrant rights director Steve Valdez-Symonds has issued these comments on Mahmoud’s visa threat. double quotation mark “Rather than threatening to impose a ban on the few Eritreans who might ever be granted a visa and be permitted to depart from that country, the Home Secretary needs to address the shocking fall in asylum grants under this Government that has got even worse on her watch. double quotation mark “Eritrea’s appalling human rights record includes arbitrarily detaining people forced to return, and indefinite and forced conscription in circumstances that in some cases amounts to slavery. double quotation mark “Politicians are once again failing us all and putting lives at risk by simply refusing to manage this country’s asylum responsibilities fairly and efficiently. That is why our asylum system is in such a mess and contributes to a toxic environment where some people are so easily stirred to anger, hate and even violence against refugees who are fleeing war or persecution.” Home Office data shows just 77 work visas were issued to Eritrean nationals in the year to June , making up 0.03% of the total of 234,841. Eritreans accounted for an even smaller proportion of study visas issued in the same period, at 0.01% (33 out of a total of 385,974). Some more on the visa ban Mahmood has threatened for Eritrean nationals to convince the east African country to take back people who haven’t passed the UK’s asylum seeker checks. Britain and Eritrea have been locked in a battle over migrant returns for months. Essentially, the UK has been trying to restore a deal that had been in place from 2024 which saw Eritrea issue emergency travel documents to nationals without a valid passport so they could be deported to their home country. But since March, Eritrea has rejected that deal. Diplomats had been trying to hash out a solution behind the scenes for months; Mahmood has now gone public with her ultimatum: double quotation mark “My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK.” Restrictions have already kicked. From today, Eritrea’s diplomats are facing limits on how far they can travel outside of London without seeking foreign office permissions. And fast-track visa processing has been halted. Andy Burnham has “apologised” and corrected the record after saying an “individual” was “responsible for the murder” of Ann Widdecombe, PA reports. The PM was accused of a “breach of the presumption of innocence” by the Tories after his comment during Prime Minister’s Questions. While No 10 declined to comment on Wednesday evening, Burnham has now corrected Hansard, the official record of government. A Downing Street spokesperson said: double quotation mark A correction has been issued to Hansard, and that will be published in due course. Asked if the PM understood the code, they said: double quotation mark The fact that we have issued an update speaks for itself. Burnham referred in the chamber to the “individual responsible for the murder” of Widdecombe – a former Conservative minister and Reform UK’s justice spokeswoman – despite the legal process still being in its early stages. John Healey has promised to use his first budget in a fortnight’s time to offer consumers and businesses a “breathing space” while sticking to Labour’s fiscal rules. Speaking to journalists in Bangkok, where he has been attending the International Monetary Fund (IMF) annual meetings, the chancellor said he was conscious of rising costs. double quotation mark I want the budget to be a budget that gives Britain a bit of breathing space – but also reinforces the strength of our fiscal plans and the strength of our resilience and our economy for the future. The government has already cut VAT on electricity bills , but Healey is expected to announce a further package of energy support at his 28 October tax and spending statement, before what is expected to be a sharp rise in the energy price cap in January . He said: double quotation mark The prime minister’s talked about recognising the cost of business, not just the cost of living. Healey also reiterated his insistence that he will be sticking to the spending plans set out by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, at last year’s spending review – and cabinet colleagues will have to find any additional resources within their existing budgets. double quotation mark When the second half of a spending review is in place, there are pressures on departments, and colleagues are doing a good job of managing with what they’ve got. You have to reprioritise if you want to do fresh things. As we’ve been reporting, former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson has been sentenced to a total of 15 years for sexual offences against two women who were children when he abused them three decades ago. You can read our full report from my colleague, Ireland correspondent Rory Carroll, here: Britain’s AI Security Institute is “no longer enough” to keep the country safe and the government should bring forward statutory AI protections, the chairman of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee has warned. Liam Byrne, the Labour former minister, said the Cyber Resilience Bill could be used to bring the statutory protections into law. It is currently making its way through Parliament, having passed its initial stages in the House of Commons earlier this year. Speaking in the Commons today, Byrne said: double quotation mark We are blessed to have the AI Security Institute in this country, but it’s no longer enough. So, will ministers confirm that we will have Government amendments at report stage of the Cyber Resilience Bill to ensure that we have statutory AI protections to keep this country safe? AI minister Kanishka Narayan said he would work with MPs across the House “on ideas for the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, looking in particular at protections on AI security”. The Scottish National Party’s conference kicks off today, and as my colleagues Patrick Greenfield and Eve Livingston write, this year even Andy Burnham has been invited But by the time John Swinney stands up to address members on Saturday afternoon in Aberdeen to reinvigorate the case for a second independence referendum, his party may regret giving the UK prime minister so much prominence in the conference buildup. Burnham is expected to visit Scotland on Friday – the middle of the event – in a thinly veiled attempt to overshadow the SNP gathering. While he will be in a different venue, the former Manchester mayor’s presence in Scotland will loom large over the event. Since taking over at No 10 in July, Burnham has largely avoided direct confrontations with his political rivals, rarely attacking Nigel Farage or Kemi Badenoch. But he has taken a different approach with the Scottish first minister. The SNP leader was the only politician from a rival party, apart from Margaret Thatcher, that Burnham mentioned in his keynote address to the Labour party conference last month. He reflected on Swinney’s prediction that he would be the last prime minister of the UK at a meeting of separatist parties Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland to mark the first time all three devolved parliaments were governed by nationalists. Swinney inadvertently did so on the day Burnham’s father died. “I quote that not to seek sympathy,” Burnham said, holding back tears. “Nor to criticise John Swinney. I relay it because I want you to know how it made me feel. Utterly determined to prove him wrong.” Beyond ruling out a second independence referendum, recent British prime ministers have often paid little attention to Scottish internal affairs. Burnham has already said there is “no clear consensus” for another vote. But unlike his predecessors, he has decided to take on the SNP by loudly make the case for the union on Scottish soil. Burnham presents a new challenge for the SNP as they seek to re-energise the case for Scottish independence . Swinney has said he wants a new vote before 2031. The separatists have grown used to facing off against rightwing, pro-Brexit governments in London during two decades in power in Holyrood, making it easier to argue that Scotland’s interests have been dismissed. Burnham’s devolution agenda, openness to exploring a return to the European Union and £2 bus fares are harder to confront. Jeffrey Donaldson, the former leader of the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) in Northern Ireland, has been sentenced to 15 years in prison for historical sexual offences against two women when they were children. My colleague Taz Ali has live coverage of the sentencing here: Donaldon led the DUP from 2021 until 2024. He was convicted in June of one count of rape, 13 counts of indecent assault and four counts of gross indecency for crimes committed between 1985 and 2008. Judge Paul Ramsey said Donaldson had “doubled down on his denials” since his conviction. “There has not been, and doubtless will not be, one word of regret, apology or shame from this man to at least provide his victims with some crumb of comfort,” he said. He added Donaldson had experienced a “catastrophic descent into disgrace”. Labour says it’s told all of its local councils who share power with the Green Party to review their agreements after the Greens passed a “Zionism is Racism” motion at their autumn conference earlier this month. If Green coalition partners don’t agree to condemn the policy, the Labour council groups have been instructed to terminate existing power deals. Yesterday Andy Burnham in PMQs condemned the Greens motion - which wasn’t supported by most of the party’s MPs, but was passed by a majority of members – as “wrong” and “antisemitic”. He ruled out Labour doing deals with the Green party: double quotation mark We cannot support a partnership with a party that holds [the] position that has recently been adopted. Following from the Zelenskyy visit to Number 10 yesterday, John Healey has wrapped up his meeting with the UK press pack in Bangkok with a heavy hint that he is preparing to offer more support to Ukraine at the budget. Healey , who was of course defence secretary earlier this year, said: “Now is the time to step up pressure on Putin and step up support for Ukraine.” Asked if that could come as soon as the budget, Healey said: “I’m working on different ways we can step up support for Ukraine, military, diplomatic, and economic, and you know, if anybody needed any reminder of that, it’s what we see coming out of Ukraine, with Putin targeting these energy systems , leaving thousands without power, as we’ve got a harsh winter approaching. The future of Ukraine is the future of European security, and that’s that’s why it’s so crucial that Putin doesn’t prevail.”d Yesterday, Andy Burnham hosted Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Number 10 in a significant show of support, after recent attacks by the Trump. The US president has swung back to hostile rhetoric against the Ukrainian leader, calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced after also announcing a deal between the US and Russia to buy cheaper diesel. He’s also ordered Ukraine to stop its long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries – something Ukraine had complied with for a few days until the Russian strikes kept coming. Zelenskyy has told the FT newspaper “we’re done” with the pause. Kyiv is also chasing answers from Washington on what has happened with a slowdown or drop-out in the military version of the Starlink satellite service - known as Starshield- which Ukraine relies upon for military operations. Elon Musk has tweeted that the service is controlled by the US government, which decides any limits on speed. Yesterday at Downing Street, PM Burnham vowed that Britain stood behind Zelenskyy and also discussed how the UK could “accelerate defensive support to Ukraine” ahead of a dreaded winter. And to another key story today on immigration – Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has warned that Eritreans could be blocked from coming to the UK unless the east African country accepts more rejected asylum seekers and criminals. As The Guardian’s Home Affairs editor Rajeev Syal writes: VIPs and officials from the east African country have already been stripped of fast-track access to UK visas after their government refused to cooperate with the return of its nationals, the home secretary said. The warning comes after Eritrea abruptly withdrew returns cooperation earlier this year, the Home Office said. The UK should not get drawn into rejecting applicants for asylum from Eritrea , refugee organisations have warned, because it is a war-torn country and the UK usually accepts the vast majority of applicants, who are often escaping famine and conflict. Eritreans were the most common nationality arriving by small boat in the year ending June 2026. Returns arrangements are vital for removing people who have been refused asylum and foreign criminals. Mahmood said: double quotation mark “Eritrea has had every chance to accept the return of criminals and those with no right to be in the UK. Unlike other countries, it has refused. “My message to the Eritrean government is simple: take back your nationals or face a complete ban on your citizens entering the UK. “I will not hesitate to impose further measures on other countries refusing to cooperate.” The move follows similar threats of visa sanctions against Angola, Namibia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2025. Angola and Namibia subsequently agreed to cooperate with demands on migrant returns, while the Democratic Republic of the Congo faced visa restrictions before reaching an agreement with the UK in February. Just over 100 refused asylum seekers from Eritrea have been deported – a figure comprising less than 4% of the 2,626 people whose claims were rejected in the past four years. Nearly 6,000 Eritreans have reached the UK across the Channel in the year to June, the highest number of any nationality. Quick reminder to anyone not super across what banks have to pay in taxes, their current rate is a 3% surcharge on profits, on top of the 25% corporation tax rate. All banks operating in the UK – both British and foreign – pay this levy, and the sector has recorded tremendous profits in recent years driven by higher interest rates. (Markets are also assessing that the central bank will most likely raise rates next month to 4%.) Taxing the big banks a little bit more has long been mooted as a voter-friendly way for Healey to raise some cash. Tory leader Kemi Badenoch is expected to joined the banks today though in criticising against the measure. The argument is that it would damage the UK finance sector’s international competitiveness, drive businesses out of the country, and/or that banks might just pass on the costs to customers. Tory shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has argued: “Britain needs growth but a raid on the financial services sector will stifle it.” Healey is meeting with UK journalists now at the IMF in Bangkok, including my colleague Heather Stewart . The August print – a 0.1% growth instead of the predicted 0.1% contraction – would have been very welcome news this morning, but he still faces a major challenge trying to find cash going into his 28 October budget. The idea of raising taxes on bank profits has been floating around, and Healey is asked on this. He replies: “I don’t want anybody to try and read in or second guess what [we may] do in two weeks’ time. My observations on the banks are just that people too often see them as a big distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future prospects. That said, you know I’ve got decisions to take in the in the budget, and I will. I’ll set those out in two weeks’ time. Healey added that his “special responsibility as Chancellor is to protect the resilience of the British economy for the future”. He also repeated comments welcoming the IMF’s support for the UK’s fiscal plans. To just go back to that GDP uptick briefly, John Healey is at the IMF/World Bank meetings in Bangkok and is due to speak shortly. I’ll bring his comments here courtesy of my colleague Graeme Wearden’s reporting over on our business live blog. Basically, the UK economy is still weak but performing slightly better than earlier gloomy predictions; the IMF in fact this week raised its growth forecast to 1.£3% – up from its April prediction of 0.8%. Analysts are saying, at this rate, the UK is on track to be the second- best- performing G7 economy this year. Entering the conference centre this morning, Healey said in brief remarks: “I’m pleased the IMF here in Bangkok have backed our economic plans in London. They say the UK stands out on growth despite the deep economic shocks that are affecting worldwide at present. They say Britain stands out on our plans to get to grips with the big borrowing costs by previous governments. They also say it’s important to stay the path, and I will follow that as I prepare my budget in two weeks’ time.” Reform leader Nigel Farage has postponed a major announcement that was due to take place in Essex this morning after an ITV investigation aired last night showing party councillors and election candidates making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views. Three councillors have already stood down from the party, which said it was conducting an investigation over the first revelations from the ITV undercover investigation. More are expected from the undercover filming of senior Reform politicians and officials working at its UK headquarters. Farage has made repeated pledges over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election. However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney , a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull , calling Asian homeowners “parasites,” and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”. Feeney won seats on Birmingham city council and S olihull Metropolitan borough council and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. He has announced that he has left Reform “for personal reasons”. Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues. Feeney was filmed with other candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, talking about where a local mosque might be built. After they make extreme racist comments in the discussion, Feeney says: “Oh god, we’re all going to end up in the papers”. Chris Whelan announced he had resigned from Reform on 12 October “on personal and health grounds”. Campbell is still in post.
